issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette: José, a 22-year-old Latin American man and HVAC technician, had experienced a traumatic event that continues to haunt him. One day at work, while he was on a routine job installing an air conditioning unit in a high-rise building, a mishap occurred. He accidentally knocked the ladder loose, causing his coworker, Luis, to fall from the third floor. The sound of the impact and Luis’s screams were seared into José's memory. Though Luis survived with severe injuries, José was overwhelmed by guilt and self-recrimination. José had come to believe that he could no longer trust his own body, which felt unreliable in moments when his physical reactions seemed out of his control. The event also left him feeling unrecognizable to himself; the person who used to be confident and competent now found it difficult to look at his reflection without seeing a stranger. He harbored deep feelings of guilt for not doing more to prevent the accident, despite being certain that he had no way to stop what happened. These negative appraisals led José to engage in maladaptive strategies such as avoiding anniversaries connected to the event and any other potential stressors. This avoidance became a habit, and it reinforced his belief that he could not trust himself or his body. He felt compelled to overanalyze every detail of the accident, trying desperately to make sense of how something so terrible could have happened under his watch. The memory of Luis falling had become alien to him; it felt like it belonged to someone else rather than to himself. When he thought about the event, he could smell the pungent scent of oil and metal from the air conditioning unit, which only intensified his sense that something dangerous was looming. This olfactory recall often triggered strong physical reactions, such as a racing heart and sweating palms, especially in moments of unusual silence. These memories began to force their way into his mind at unexpected times, leading José to feel an ever-present threat. He developed the belief that he could only feel safe within a very limited number of places, primarily his home or familiar environments. This sense of threat was further exacerbated by any reminders of the event, such as working on ladders or hearing similar metallic sounds. Over time, this cycle tightened. José’s overanalyzing and avoidance behaviors reinforced his negative appraisals, creating a self-reinforcing loop that kept him in a constant state of hypervigilance and anxiety. He found it increasingly difficult to concentrate at work, which led to more stress and further avoidance behaviors. His relationships suffered as well; he pushed away friends and coworkers who tried to engage with him, fearing they might see the unrecognizable self he now perceived. José’s current state was marked by a profound sense of isolation and guilt. He had finally sought help after realizing that his attempts at coping were only making things worse. What frightened him most was the fear that he would never be able to forgive himself for what happened, and the constant worry that something equally dangerous might happen again. Despite this, he was hopeful that with support, he could find a way to reclaim control over his life and begin to trust himself once more.
